Data::Denormalization.sourceTitle: Decoupling table relationships during database decomposition
Data::Denormalization.summary: Denormalization intentionally duplicates selected data across tables or records to simplify frequent reads and avoid joins. The tradeoff is extra storage and the need to keep copies synchronized.
Data::Denormalization.explanation: Denormalization intentionally stores selected fields redundantly in a read-oriented record or projection. Reads become simpler and can avoid joins, but every copied value creates additional write and consistency work when the source changes.

example.title: A denormalized read model
example.explanation: This runnable example shows a read-optimized projection that stores the fields a catalog query needs, avoiding a join at read time.

useCases.title: Avoid repeated joins
useCases.scenario: A read-heavy endpoint repeatedly combines the same related tables.

useCases.title: Build a read model
useCases.scenario: A service needs a consolidated product view containing product, pricing, and inventory fields.

useCases.title: Optimize hot access paths
useCases.scenario: Frequently accessed fields improve performance when stored close to the requesting record.

keyPoints: Denormalization deliberately duplicates related data instead of keeping every fact in one normalized location.
Choose duplicated fields from observed, frequent access patterns rather than duplicating an entire model.
Treat denormalization as selective optimization, not an all-or-nothing database design rule.
A consolidated read model can hold the fields needed by a common request and eliminate repeated joins.
Normalization minimizes redundancy; denormalization accepts redundancy to optimize access.
gotchas: Do not denormalize automatically: update and delete costs can outweigh faster queries.
Use selective duplication based on measured access patterns and a clear performance or dependency benefit.

Data::Partitioning and sharding.sourceTitle: Design a data partitioning strategy - Azure
Data::Partitioning and sharding.summary: Partition data horizontally by a shard (partition) key so each shard holds a subset of rows and workload spreads across multiple stores. Choose a key that distributes work evenly and supports efficient routing.
Data::Partitioning and sharding.explanation: Horizontal partitioning divides rows among stores with the same schema, using a partition or shard key to determine placement. A well-chosen key distributes workload across shards, while including that key in requests lets routing direct operations to the relevant shard; related data can use the same key to preserve locality and support coordinated access.

example.title: Hash a shard key
example.explanation: This deterministic shard-key function maps each customer to one of four shards; production systems should use a well-tested hash and routing layer.

useCases.title: Scale storage horizontally
useCases.scenario: Distribute a large dataset across multiple database stores.

useCases.title: Increase throughput
useCases.scenario: Spread requests across machines to reduce contention.

useCases.title: Preserve data locality
useCases.scenario: Keep related records together by using the same partition key.

keyPoints: Horizontal partitioning places subsets of rows in multiple stores while keeping their schemas consistent.
A shard is one partition containing the rows selected by partition-key values.
The shard key may be one attribute or a combination of attributes, and it determines placement.
The shard key is central to distributing data and workload evenly.
Shard key and partition key are alternative names for the routing attribute.
Key selection is the primary design decision because it controls distribution.
For example, product inventory can be divided according to product key values.
gotchas: Choose the shard key carefully because changing it after deployment can be difficult.
A key that creates uneven partitions can overload individual shards and undermine scalability.
Sharding spreads work across machines, but it does not remove the need to evaluate contention and workload distribution.

Data::Relational versus non-relational.sourceTitle: What is a NoSQL Database? - AWS
Data::Relational versus non-relational.summary: Choose relational databases for structured, strongly consistent transactional workloads and rich relationships. Choose non-relational databases for flexible models, horizontal scale, and access patterns that favor low latency over full relational guarantees.
Data::Relational versus non-relational.explanation: Start with the workload's access patterns and consistency requirements. Use a relational store when structured data, relationships, joins, and multi-row ACID transactions matter; use a non-relational store when flexible data models, horizontal scale, or narrowly defined low-latency access patterns matter. Non-relational designs commonly shape records around reads instead of joining data at query time.

example.title: Direct key-based lookup
example.explanation: A key-value-style access pattern retrieves one user directly by identifier without joining tables.

useCases.title: Strongly consistent transactions
useCases.scenario: Order checkout, inventory updates, or financial transactions requiring atomic multi-step changes.

useCases.title: Low-latency key access
useCases.scenario: User profiles, sessions, or other records retrieved directly by a stable key.

useCases.title: Flexible data models
useCases.scenario: Rapidly evolving or heterogeneous records that do not fit one rigid schema.

useCases.title: Horizontal scale
useCases.scenario: Large workloads designed to distribute across multiple database nodes.

keyPoints: Relational databases are a strong fit for transactional workloads that require ACID guarantees.
Choose a non-relational store when predictable, low-latency access patterns are more important than relational querying.
Relational databases use an explicit schema covering tables, columns, indexes, and relationships.
Non-relational models are useful when schema flexibility and horizontal scaling outweigh full relational guarantees.
gotchas: Do not assume a non-relational database provides the same transactional guarantees as a relational database; verify its consistency and transaction scope.
A non-relational schema should not be designed before the application's reads and writes are known.

Data::Replication.sourceTitle: Amazon DocumentDB High availability and replication
Data::Replication.summary: Replication copies updates from a primary to replica instances, improving availability and allowing read traffic to scale horizontally. Replicas are eventually consistent, so reads can lag behind recent writes.
Data::Replication.explanation: Replication maintains replica instances from a primary so applications can distribute read-only queries and improve availability. Because updates reach replicas asynchronously, replica reads can be stale; monitor lag and size or scale replicas when writes or query load cause them to fall behind.

example.title: Route reads to replicas
example.explanation: Illustrates routing read-only work to a replicated database cluster; the exact client configuration depends on the deployment.

useCases.title: Read scaling
useCases.scenario: Distribute read-only queries across replica instances for a read-heavy application.

useCases.title: Higher availability
useCases.scenario: Keep serving reads through a primary-instance restart or failure.

useCases.title: Workload isolation
useCases.scenario: Separate long-running analytical reads from primary write traffic.

keyPoints: Use replica instances to improve availability and distribute read traffic.
Replicas are suited to read-heavy workloads because their capacity is dedicated to reads.
Under normal conditions, replica results usually follow primary writes quickly.
Typical lag is low, but it varies with workload and is not a freshness guarantee.
Add replicas to distribute read demand when replicas themselves are overloaded.
gotchas: Reads from replicas may return data that does not yet include the primary's latest writes.
Heavy write throughput can increase replication lag and make replica data less current.
Long-running reads can compete with replication work and increase lag.
Excessive concurrent reads can overload replicas and delay replication.

Distributed systems::Clock and ordering.summary: Avoid synchronized wall clocks as a correctness mechanism in distributed systems: imperfect synchronization makes them unreliable for ordering and coordination. Use wall-clock time for human consumption, and local elapsed durations when leases require time.
Distributed systems::Clock and ordering.explanation: In a distributed system, machines can disagree about wall-clock time because synchronization is imperfect and clocks can drift. Therefore, do not use synchronized wall-clock timestamps to coordinate operations or establish correctness. If leases require time, measure a local elapsed duration rather than depending on a globally agreed wall-clock value.

example.code: // No runnable code is needed: the documented design rule is architectural.
example.explanation: The rule is to avoid using synchronized wall-clock readings for distributed correctness or ordering; use local elapsed durations where a time-based lease is necessary.

useCases.title: Use logical or protocol-based ordering instead of wall-clock timestamps.

useCases.title: Avoid requiring servers to agree on the current wall-clock time.

useCases.title: Measure a local elapsed duration rather than relying on synchronized wall-clock time.
useCases.scenario: Implementing leases

keyPoints: Do not make distributed correctness depend on wall-clock time.
Synchronized clocks are not a dependable basis for ordering events across machines.
Avoid using clock agreement to coordinate distributed operations.
Use wall-clock time for human-facing purposes such as timestamps and diagnostics, not algorithmic correctness.
When a lease needs time, use a duration measured locally by the participating machine.
gotchas: Clock synchronization may not be accurate enough across a cluster for ordering or coordinating distributed operations.
Time-based leases still require care; the documented alternative is local elapsed duration, not synchronized wall-clock time.
Prefer elapsed durations to avoid failures caused by clock drift and disagreement about global time.

Distributed systems::Consensus.sourceTitle: Quorum queues for RabbitMQ on Amazon MQ
Distributed systems::Consensus.summary: Consensus enables replicas to agree on a leader and on replicated decisions. Leader election handles failures, while a majority quorum prevents unsafe progress when too few replicas are available.
Distributed systems::Consensus.explanation: Consensus coordinates replicas so they agree on one leader and on committed data. A leader typically proposes changes, followers replicate and vote, and a majority quorum makes a decision; if the leader fails, the remaining replicas elect a replacement. This preserves consistency and allows continued operation only when enough members remain.

example.title: Majority-based leader failover
example.explanation: A minimal runnable illustration of electing a replacement leader only when enough replicas remain to form a quorum.

useCases.title: Fault-tolerant messaging
useCases.scenario: Replicated queues need to remain available after a broker failure.

useCases.title: Distributed coordination
useCases.scenario: Several instances must coordinate exclusive work or shared state.

useCases.title: Consistent replication
useCases.scenario: Replicas must agree before accepting a replicated write.

keyPoints: A consensus group commonly has one leader and one or more follower replicas.
Leader election lets replicas select a replacement leader after failure, using a majority decision.
After failover, surviving replicas continue replication under the newly elected leader.
Routing writes through one leader prevents competing replicas from concurrently making authoritative updates.
Leader election and distributed locking require a strongly consistent coordination mechanism.
gotchas: A leader failure requires a majority vote to elect a replacement; without a majority, progress cannot safely continue.
Replica placement across failure domains helps maintain availability when one node is lost.

Distributed systems::Distributed transac.summary: Prefer sagas for distributed workflows spanning service-owned databases. Execute local transactions, then use continuation or compensating transactions to recover from failures instead of relying on two-phase commit.
Distributed systems::Distributed transac.explanation: A saga coordinates a distributed workflow as local transactions. Each successful step enables the next; when a later step fails, compensating transactions reverse the completed work. This avoids requiring a single coordinator for two-phase commit across separate service databases, but reaches consistency through recovery rather than one atomic commit.

example.title: Minimal saga with compensation
example.explanation: A minimal saga executes local steps and compensates completed steps in reverse order if a later step fails.

useCases.title: E-commerce checkout
useCases.scenario: Order, inventory, and payment services must complete a business workflow across separate databases.

useCases.title: Resource provisioning
useCases.scenario: A multi-step provisioning workflow can fail after earlier resources were created.

useCases.title: Long-running business process
useCases.scenario: A long-running process crosses service or trust boundaries and cannot hold a distributed lock.

keyPoints: Model the distributed operation as ordered local transactions, each owned by its service.
On failure, undo completed effects with compensating transactions rather than rolling back every database atomically.
Use continuation for retrying and progressing after infrastructure failures; use compensation for reversing business effects.
Database-per-service architectures generally cannot use relational two-phase commit as their cross-service transaction mechanism.
A successful local update starts the next step, commonly through an event or message.
Orchestration centralizes workflow coordination in an orchestrator.
gotchas: Failure handling may choose retry/forward recovery or compensation, so operations need explicit recovery behavior.

Distributed systems::Idempotency.summary: Idempotency makes repeated identical requests have the same effect as one request. An idempotency token lets a service recognize retries, prevent duplicate side effects, and return the original response.
Distributed systems::Idempotency.explanation: The client creates a unique token for a logical request and sends that same token on every retry. The service records the token with the operation’s result; a repeated token returns the stored response instead of applying the mutation again. This lets clients retry after timeouts or connection failures without duplicate records or side effects.

parameters.name: idempotency token
parameters.description: A client-generated idempotency token identifying one logical request; the same token is sent when the request is repeated.

Distributed systems::Idempotency.returns: The original response for a repeated token; a newly processed response for a new token.

example.title: Retrying a payment safely
example.explanation: The client reuses the same idempotency key when retrying the request, allowing the service to return the original result without creating another payment.

useCases.title: Prevent duplicate payments
useCases.scenario: A client times out after submitting a payment and retries the request.

useCases.title: Deduplicate repeated deliveries
useCases.scenario: A message or API request may be delivered more than once.

useCases.title: Make mutating APIs retryable
useCases.scenario: A service mutates state but clients need safe retry behavior after transient failures.

keyPoints: Idempotency makes repeated delivery of one logical request converge on one mutation, even when the network causes retries.
A client supplies a token that identifies the logical operation across attempts.
The service checks the token before deciding whether to execute the operation.
A duplicate request returns the previously stored result instead of applying the side effect again.
The first request performs the operation and records its result for later retries.
gotchas: The replayed response may reflect the original completed request rather than current resource state.

Framing the problem::Constraints and ass.summary: Write down the assumptions behind an architecture and define how to test them. Challenge unverified assumptions, while checking both explicit and implied requirements.
Framing the problem::Constraints and ass.explanation: Record architectural assumptions explicitly, then test or verify them instead of relying on unverified beliefs. Revisit assumptions as requirements and the design evolve, and check both explicit and implied requirements.

keyPoints: List the assumptions that influence architectural decisions and attach a way to test each one.
Use an explicit review question to expose assumptions that might otherwise remain implicit.
Check that the architecture addresses both stated requirements and requirements inferred from context.
Avoid adding complexity merely to cover speculative needs; keep the design proportional to known requirements.
Expect constraints, requirements, and implementation choices to change, so make assumptions easy to revisit.
gotchas: Unverified assumptions can make the architecture fragile; document how each assumption will be tested or verified.
Treat the design as evolutionary rather than assuming the initial architecture can capture every future detail.

Framing the problem::Functional requirem.summary: Functional requirements state what a system must do and how users experience its behavior. Define them through user journeys, record who/what/why, split large requirements, and specify how satisfaction will be verified before selecting implementation technologies.
Framing the problem::Functional requirem.explanation: Start with the user journey and express each requirement as observable behavior: who performs an action, what the system does, and why it matters. Break oversized requirements into smaller ones, define how each is satisfied, and capture exceptional paths as well as the successful path. Keep these statements focused on behavior rather than implementation so they can guide later design choices.

keyPoints: Describe required system behavior and capabilities, not the technologies used to implement them.
For every requirement, identify the actor, the system behavior, and the reason the behavior is needed.
Define observable acceptance criteria so the team can tell when each requirement is complete.
gotchas: Avoid requirements that bundle too much behavior; split them into smaller, independently understandable parts.

Framing the problem::Non-functional requ.summary: Non-functional requirements specify how well a system must operate, including measurable goals for latency, availability, durability, and consistency. State them explicitly because they shape architecture and technology choices.
Framing the problem::Non-functional requ.explanation: Treat non-functional requirements as measurable quality targets that describe how well a system must operate, not merely what it must do. Capture them per important user or system flow, then use them to guide architecture and technology choices.

Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes and operational expectations rather than business behavior.
Explicitly identify scalability, availability, and latency targets during problem framing.
Use the targets to select architecture patterns, infrastructure, and data technologies.
Record requirements per flow because availability, scalability, consistency, and recovery needs can vary.
gotchas: Do not assume one target fits every flow; critical paths may need different availability, consistency, or recovery guarantees.

Framing the problem::Read and write rati.sourceTitle: PERF03-BP01 Use a purpose-built data store that best supports your data access and storage requirements
Framing the problem::Read and write rati.summary: Use the read/write ratio and access pattern to choose data stores and scaling techniques. Read-heavy workloads often benefit from caching or read replicas; write-heavy workloads need write-optimized designs.
Framing the problem::Read and write rati.explanation: Measure the proportion of read queries relative to writes, then choose storage and scaling mechanisms that fit the dominant pattern. Read-heavy workloads commonly benefit from caching or read replicas, while write-heavy workloads require designs optimized for write throughput and consistency.

    strategy="prioritize write throughput and failover"

Quantify the read-to-write ratio as an explicit input to architecture decisions.
For read-dominant traffic, add a caching layer when repeated reads can be served without hitting the primary store.
Relational systems can scale read traffic by sending reads to replicas instead of the primary database.
When reads are complex and require consistency, use a relational option such as Amazon RDS.
The workload's read/write character should influence the multi-Region topology.

Reliability & operations::Capacity and c.summary: Capacity and cost depend on the pricing model: pay-per-use follows requests and duration, while provisioned capacity charges for reserved resources. Per-request pricing suits variable traffic but can cost more than provisioned capacity at sustained, high throughput.
Reliability & operations::Capacity and c.explanation: Choose a pricing model that matches traffic shape. Per-request pricing scales with invocations and can become costly at very high throughput, while reserved or provisioned capacity may be cheaper for sustained, predictable demand; dynamic allocation avoids paying for idle capacity when demand is uncertain.

keyPoints: Pay-per-use models charge for actual invocations and execution duration, avoiding idle-capacity charges.
Estimate request cost from two dimensions: invocation count and execution duration.
Capacity-based pricing charges for reserved compute or throughput rather than only completed requests.
Hybrid models provide request-based billing that grows linearly with traffic and require no upfront capacity commitment.
Compare cumulative request charges with reserved capacity when traffic is steady enough to forecast.
Automatic scaling can align spend with variable demand and reduce charges for unused capacity.
gotchas: Reserved or provisioned capacity can cost money during quiet periods; use it when demand is sustained and predictable.
Per-request pricing may lose its cost advantage at very high throughput.

Reliability & operations::Circuit breake.summary: Circuit breakers stop repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency, while bulkheads constrain work to isolated, fixed-size capacity. Together they prevent dependency failures or overload from consuming the whole application.
Reliability & operations::Circuit breake.explanation: A circuit breaker stops calls to a dependency after failures exceed a threshold, then periodically permits a trial call before restoring traffic. A bulkhead isolates work into bounded resource pools or queues so one failing or overloaded dependency cannot consume capacity needed by other operations.

An open breaker should allow limited probe calls after a delay to test recovery.
A successful probe closes the breaker and restores normal traffic.

Reliability & operations::Failure modes.summary: Failure mode analysis enumerates where a workload can fail and which flows, components, customers, regions, or business processes each failure can affect. This exposes blast radius and guides mitigation design.
Reliability & operations::Failure modes.explanation: Failure mode analysis examines critical workload flows component by component, identifies possible failure types, and records their blast radius so mitigations can reduce widespread impact.

Consider regional outages, availability-zone outages, service outages, attacks, misconfiguration, and operator error.
A regional outage can remove all workload components and flows hosted in that region.
A zone outage affects components and flows that depend on that zone.
A service outage affects flows that require the unavailable service and may affect their dependents.

Reliability & operations::Observability.summary: Observability uses metrics, logs, traces, and events to understand system behavior and reliability. Define health indicators first, then collect structured, contextual telemetry and correlate it across components for diagnosis.
Reliability & operations::Observability.explanation: Observability combines telemetry from metrics, logs, and traces to reveal system health and behavior. Define health indicators first, then collect structured, contextual signals from every component and connect them so dashboards, alerts, and investigations can explain failures and bottlenecks.

example.title: Emit the three observability signals
example.code:
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server
import logging
from opentelemetry import trace

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
requests = Counter("requests_total", "Total requests")
latency = Histogram("request_latency_seconds", "Request latency")
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

@latency.time()
def handle_request():
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("handle_request"):
        requests.inc()
        logging.info("request handled")

start_http_server(8000)
handle_request()
example.explanation: This small service emits a metric, a structured operational log, and a trace span so the signals can be correlated during diagnosis.

The monitoring stack runs alongside the functional stack and analyzes workload behavior in production.
Traces expose request journeys and problems spanning multiple services.

Keep schemas and context consistent, including the emitting component and timestamps.

Reliability & operations::Rate limiting.sourceTitle: REL05-BP02 Throttle requests - AWS Well-Architected Framework
Reliability & operations::Rate limiting.summary: Throttle incoming requests to prevent resource exhaustion during demand spikes. Token-bucket limits allow controlled rates and bounded bursts, while throttled clients retry later instead of amplifying overload.
Reliability & operations::Rate limiting.explanation: Rate limiting caps request volume or operation size over time so a downstream service stays within capacity. A token bucket permits bursts up to its bucket size, then rejects excess requests; callers should interpret overload signals, avoid retry storms, and retry later with bounded randomized delay.
Reliability & operations::Rate limiting.returns: A request is admitted when capacity is available; otherwise it is rejected with a throttling indication such as HTTP 429.

example.title: Token-bucket admission control
example.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from time import monotonic

@dataclass
class TokenBucket:
    rate: float
    capacity: float
    tokens: float = 0
    updated: float = monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1) -> bool:
        now = monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens < cost:
            return False
        self.tokens -= cost
        return True

bucket = TokenBucket(rate=5, capacity=10, tokens=10)
print(bucket.allow())
example.explanation: This runnable token-bucket example admits requests while tokens are available and rejects excess demand until tokens refill.

keyPoints: Use throttling to shed excess demand before resource exhaustion causes broader failure.
Accept requests under the configured rate and reject excess requests with an explicit throttling response.
A token bucket models a steady rate while allowing bounded bursts.
Consumers should treat throttling as a recoverable overload signal and retry later rather than immediately flooding the service.
gotchas: Coordinate retries with rate limiting, and use few retries with small randomized delays.

Scaling & performance::Asynchronous proc.sourceTitle: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern - Azure Architecture Center
Scaling & performance::Asynchronous proc.summary: Use a queue as a buffer between request handling and slow work. The producer enqueues the required data and returns quickly, while a consumer processes messages asynchronously at its own pace.
Scaling & performance::Asynchronous proc.explanation: A queue separates request handling from slow work: the producer posts a message, and a consumer retrieves and processes it later. This lets the consumer work at its own pace and absorbs bursts between producers and services.
Scaling & performance::Asynchronous proc.returns: The request receives an acknowledgment after the message is placed on the queue; the eventual processing result is not returned through the original synchronous path.

example.title: Queue work for an asynchronous consumer
example.code:
from queue import Queue
from threading import Thread

jobs = Queue()

def worker():
    while True:
        job = jobs.get()
        if job is None:
            break
        process(job)
        jobs.task_done()

def process(job):
    print(f"processed {job}")

Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
jobs.put({"transaction_id": "t-123"})
print("accepted")
example.explanation: The request path enqueues a small job and immediately acknowledges it; a worker later retrieves and processes the job.

useCases.title: Smooth intermittent load
useCases.scenario: Burst traffic temporarily exceeds worker capacity.

useCases.title: Keep the request path responsive
useCases.scenario: A request triggers slow or resource-intensive work.

useCases.title: Decouple producers and consumers
useCases.scenario: Several producers submit work to a shared worker pool.

keyPoints: Put a durable queue between the request handler and the slow worker to remove the work from the request path.
The producer should enqueue the inputs the consumer needs, preferably as a compact job description.
Consumers pull jobs, execute the slow operation, and acknowledge or remove completed messages according to the queue system.
Decoupling lets workers scale independently and process bursts without forcing each request to wait.
One queue can absorb variable demand from many producers before workers process the accumulated jobs.
gotchas: Queues reduce overload, but queued work can still become stale or time out if consumers fall behind.
The caller cannot expect the slow operation's result through the original request path; use a separate status or notification mechanism when needed.
Queue storage and retention affect how long unprocessed work remains available, so configure them for the workload.

Scaling & performance::Caching strategie.summary: Choose cache-aside for on-demand reads, write-through for immediate cache freshness, or write-behind when lower write latency and delayed persistence fit the workload.
Scaling & performance::Caching strategie.explanation: Cache-aside loads data only after a cache miss and commonly invalidates the cached item after a data-store update. Write-through updates the data store and cache during the same write, while write-behind postpones the data-store write; choose based on freshness, write latency, and durability requirements.

example.title: Cache-aside read path
example.explanation: This cache-aside example checks the cache first, loads a miss from the database, and then stores the result for later reads.

useCases.title: On-demand reads with cache-aside
useCases.scenario: Read-heavy data where avoiding unnecessary cache population matters.

useCases.title: Fresh reads with write-through
useCases.scenario: Read-after-write freshness is more important than minimum write latency.

useCases.title: Lower-latency writes with write-behind
useCases.scenario: Write-intensive workloads can tolerate delayed persistence.

keyPoints: Cache-aside populates the cache on demand: read the database after a miss, then cache the returned value.
Write-through updates the cache as part of the write path, keeping subsequent reads fresh.
A cache-aside read starts with the cache and consults the database only when the key is absent.
Write-behind writes to the cache first and persists to the database later, reducing synchronous write latency.
gotchas: Write-behind can improve write-heavy performance, but delayed persistence requires careful handling of failures and durability.

Scaling & performance::Vertical and hori.sourceTitle: Architecture strategies for optimizing scaling and partitioning - Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework
Scaling & performance::Vertical and hori.summary: Vertical scaling increases capacity within an existing resource; horizontal scaling adds instances to distribute work. Match the method to the bottleneck: scale up for single-instance resource limits, or scale out when work can be distributed and resiliency matters.
Scaling & performance::Vertical and hori.explanation: Vertical scaling increases the capacity of an existing resource, such as moving to a larger server. Horizontal scaling adds instances and distributes work across them. Choose based on the bottleneck: use vertical scaling when one instance needs more CPU or memory; use horizontal scaling when the workload can be distributed across multiple nodes and needs greater capacity or resiliency.

example.code: # No runnable snippet: this concept is documented without a single universal command or API.
example.explanation: Scaling is selected by changing one resource or adding multiple resources; the exact implementation depends on the workload.

useCases.title: Increase one instance
useCases.scenario: A single server is CPU- or memory-bound and the workload cannot yet be distributed.

useCases.title: Distribute load
useCases.scenario: Traffic or workload can be served by multiple application instances.

useCases.title: Scale for availability
useCases.scenario: A service needs higher capacity and improved resilience across nodes.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, increases capacity by adding instances.
Use vertical scaling when the bottleneck responds to more CPU, memory, or similar capacity on one instance.
Use horizontal scaling when work can be distributed and the system needs more capacity, traffic handling, or resiliency.

Working through a design::Clarifying que.summary: Clarifying questions turn an open design prompt into concrete knowledge about users, workflows, pain points, desired outcomes, and important existing capabilities. Start broadly, then confirm your understanding by restating the answers.
Working through a design::Clarifying que.explanation: Clarifying questions turn an underspecified design request into explicit information about users, current processes, problems, and desired outcomes. Start broadly so stakeholders can describe their needs, then probe the existing solution and restate the answers to confirm shared understanding.

example.title: Start with open-ended questions
example.code:
questions = [
    "Who will use the system?",
    "What process should it support?",
    "What problem should it solve?"
]

for question in questions:
    print(question)
example.explanation: A minimal runnable prompt for collecting user, process, and problem requirements.

useCases.title: Discover user context
useCases.scenario: A stakeholder gives only a high-level product idea.

useCases.title: Identify non-regression requirements
useCases.scenario: A replacement system must preserve important behavior.

useCases.title: Align understanding
useCases.scenario: Different stakeholders describe the problem differently.

keyPoints: Use multiple questions to uncover users’ needs before deciding how to build the system.
Identify the people who will use the system.
Ask which workflows the system must support.
Find the main pain point in the current process.
Clarify the intended outcome of the proposed system.
Discover which existing capability must not regress.
gotchas: Do not begin with a narrow solution proposal; let stakeholders describe their context and needs first.
Confirm your interpretation by paraphrasing what stakeholders said.

Working through a design::Evolving the d.summary: As traffic grows by two orders of magnitude, evolve from a single tightly coupled deployment toward horizontally scaled, independently deployable components. Remove bottlenecks, offload expensive work, and automate capacity changes using live metrics.
Working through a design::Evolving the d.explanation: When traffic grows substantially, redesign around horizontal scaling rather than only making one machine larger. Split the system into independently scalable components, keep application instances stateless, distribute requests with load balancing, move expensive work to asynchronous background processing, and use autoscaling driven by live usage metrics.

example.title: Stateless horizontally scalable service
example.explanation: A stateless endpoint can run on multiple instances behind a load balancer, allowing capacity to grow by adding replicas.

useCases.title: Scale-out web tier
useCases.scenario: Web traffic increases substantially and front-end instances must be added without changing application behavior.

useCases.title: Independent component scaling
useCases.scenario: One workload becomes hot while other workloads remain lightly used.

useCases.title: Background job offloading
useCases.scenario: CPU-intensive processing competes with interactive requests.

useCases.title: Metric-driven autoscaling
useCases.scenario: Traffic varies unpredictably throughout the day.

keyPoints: Prefer horizontal scaling: add or remove instances as demand changes instead of relying solely on larger machines.
Separate workloads with different scaling needs so each can receive the capacity it requires.
Use autonomous, decoupled components and asynchronous communication to scale overloaded parts independently.
Give components independent state and communicate changes through events to reduce cross-component coupling.
Offload CPU- or I/O-heavy work to background jobs so front-end request handling remains responsive.
Configure autoscaling from live usage metrics and prefer the platform's built-in autoscaling capabilities.
gotchas: Adding instances does not solve bottlenecks or synchronization points; identify and remove those constraints first.
Do not scale out blindly before locating the component that limits throughput.
Use flow control and graceful degradation when demand exceeds available capacity.

Working through a design::High-level dia.sourceTitle: Create architecture design diagrams - Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework
Working through a design::High-level dia.summary: A high-level system diagram gives a broad view of a workload by showing its main components, relationships, and general data flow. Use it before refining the design into concrete technologies and integration points.
Working through a design::High-level dia.explanation: Start with a broad workload view: identify the principal components, show their relationships, and draw arrows for interaction and dependency direction. Keep implementation technologies abstract at this stage; later, refine the blocks into concrete services and integration points.
Working through a design::High-level dia.returns: A high-level system diagram showing major components, their relationships, and the general direction of data flow.

example.title: High-level system sketch
example.code:
```text
Client → API → Service → Database
          ↓
       Queue → Worker
```
example.explanation: A runnable text sketch showing major components and directional data flow before technology details are chosen.

useCases.title: Establish the overall shape
useCases.scenario: Beginning a system-design exercise

useCases.title: Communicate architecture quickly
useCases.scenario: Explaining an existing workload

useCases.title: Bound a major workload section
useCases.scenario: Planning a subsystem

useCases.title: Create a refinement baseline
useCases.scenario: Preparing detailed design work

keyPoints: Use the diagram to frame the whole system or one meaningful subsystem, not an isolated implementation detail.
Include only the major building blocks, how they relate, and the broad path data takes between them.
Draw directed arrows so readers can distinguish data movement, calls, and dependency direction.
Treat the high-level diagram as an abstraction layer that can later be refined into concrete technologies and integrations.
When data behavior needs more detail, extend the sketch to show transformations, storage, and system exits.
gotchas: Do not jump directly to a technology-specific component diagram; first establish the generic block-level structure.
Use arrows deliberately: an undirected connection does not communicate which component initiates interaction or depends on another.

Working through a design::Identifying bo.summary: Identify which resource or dependency saturates first, then limit traffic on that dimension at the relevant boundary. Continuously measure saturation and adapt limits as traffic changes.
Working through a design::Identifying bo.explanation: Identify the resource or dependency that reaches its limit first at each enforcement boundary. Measure signals such as concurrent requests, queue depth, CPU, memory, and downstream limits; then enforce a limit on that dimension and adapt it as traffic changes.

example.title: Throttle at the first saturated dimension
example.explanation: This runnable example checks multiple saturation signals and throttles on the first exhausted limit.

useCases.title: Protect an overloaded service
useCases.scenario: An API's concurrent work reaches its safe maximum before request rate does.

useCases.title: Control queue pressure
useCases.scenario: A partition's queue depth grows faster than workers can drain it.

useCases.title: Respect dependency limits
useCases.scenario: A downstream dependency imposes a quota below the application's throughput.

keyPoints: Find the first exhausted resource or dependency and throttle according to that dimension.
Use fast signals from infrastructure, application state, and per-principal activity to detect saturation.
Continuously measure, enforce limits at explicit boundaries, and adjust limits when traffic patterns change.
Candidate bottlenecks include in-flight concurrency, queues, compute resources, and downstream quotas.
gotchas: Do not assume request rate is the bottleneck; inspect concurrency, queue depth, CPU, memory, and dependency limits.
Evaluate saturation at every relevant boundary, not only at the gateway.
